name: The Adobe and Rammed-Earth Module

authority.source: Bainbridge Bunting, Early Architecture in New Mexico, University of New Mexico Press, 1976, for the measured survey; Paul Graham McHenry, Jr., Adobe and Rammed Earth Buildings: Design and Construction, Wiley, 1984, for the wall physics; the New Mexico Earthen Building Materials Code, 14.7.4 NMAC, for the ratios as a modern jurisdiction states them; Rexford Newcomb, Spanish-Colonial Architecture in the United States, 1937, and the HABS measured drawings for New Mexico and California, for the buildings themselves
authority.author: after Bainbridge Bunting and Paul Graham McHenry, Jr.
authority.note: RECONSTRUCTED, and the distinction matters more here than usual. There is no treatise: an adobe mason worked from a mould, a plumb bob and the wall his father built, and nothing in the Spanish colonial world wrote the system down. What exists is (a) measured survey of surviving fabric, principally Bunting's, (b) a modern technical literature that recovered the physics after the fact, principally McHenry's, and (c) one American building code that regulates unstabilised earth as a material at all, New Mexico's. The third of those is the dangerous one to cite, because a code figure LOOKS like a historical measurement and is not: 14.7.4 NMAC is a twentieth-century codification of what the surviving walls happen to do, in the same relation to adobe practice that Vignola stands in to Roman work. Where a figure below comes from the code rather than from the fabric, its note says so. No url is given because none of the three primary sources is freely readable online, and a plausible link would be worse than none.

module.name: One adobe laid as a header: the least thickness of a load-bearing earth wall, and the unit every horizontal dimension in the system is counted in
module.note: The part is the inch, because adobes were struck in a wooden mould and every attested standard size is in whole inches -- 10 x 14 x 4 (the New Mexico standard), 8 x 16 x 4, 12 x 18 x 4. The module is the brick's LONG dimension because that is the dimension that crosses the wall: an adobe wall is not laid in wythes the way brick is, it is laid as a bed of headers, and its thickness therefore comes in whole bricks and cannot come in anything else. One module is the thinnest bearing wall this system builds. TWO is what a house actually has -- two headers and the joint between them make 29 in, which is why every measured survey of New Mexico and Californian houses reports 24-36 in and never reports 20. THREE is a church, a placita wall, or the ground storey under a second one. RAMMED EARTH (tapia, pise) has no brick and therefore no module of its own; it is formed between shutters at whatever thickness the shutters are set to. It is carried by this pack because its wall behaves identically once built -- same slenderness limit, same reveal, same failure at the base -- and because the Iberian and Californian traditions used the two interchangeably within one building. Where a figure below is true only of the moulded brick and not of the rammed wall, the note says which.

members.name: Stone or fired-brick base course, grade to above the splash line
members.note: 12 in. An earth wall does not fail at the top. It fails at the bottom, from rising damp drawn up out of the ground and from rain splashing back off the ground within about a foot of the face, and it fails there whether or not anything is wrong with the rest of it. The stone footing carried above grade is the single most important member in the assembly and it is the one most often left off a revival building, because in a revival the wall is frame and there is nothing to protect. Set slightly proud of the wall face so water leaves the wall rather than running down it.

members.name: Wall from the base course to the window sill
members.note: 18 in, putting the sill 30 in above the floor. Higher than an Anglo-American sill, and for a reason that is about the wall rather than about the view: every inch of opening is wall that is not there, and in a bearing wall carrying a heavy earth roof the material below the sill is doing work.

members.name: The window zone -- sill to head
members.note: 42 in of clear opening height, head at 72 in above the floor. Doors are taller and take their own lintel above this line, which is why an adobe elevation does not have the single unbroken head line an Anglo-American one has; the door head and the window head are two levels and the tradition never reconciles them, exactly as the node records say the portal posts and the wall openings are never reconciled either.

members.name: Lintel and the courses that make up to the viga bearing
members.note: 18 in, bringing the underside of the vigas to 90 in -- 7 ft 6 in, the bottom of the 7 ft 6 in to 9 ft 0 in band the surviving houses show. The lintel itself is a hewn timber, always; there is no arch here and no relieving course, and the courses above the lintel are what spread the roof load off it.

members.name: Vigas, latillas and the earth roof above them
members.note: 22 in: a peeled round viga of about 9 in, latillas or split cedar of 2 in laid across it, and about 11 in of brush, earth and torta above that. The whole of it is a single structural and thermal layer and it weighs on the order of 80-100 lb per square foot, which is the reason the walls are what they are. A revival building that draws a viga and then frames the roof behind it has kept the one member that is visible and dropped the load that explains every other dimension in this pack.

members.name: Parapet above the roof, with the canales through it
members.note: 21 in, inside the 12-24 in the surveys report. The parapet is not a screen for the roof. It is the upstand that makes the roof a shallow basin so that water can only leave it through the canales, at points the builder chose, clear of the wall face -- which is the whole of the drainage design. A parapet lower than the roof build-up plus its own fall is not a parapet, it is a coping, and the water will find the wall head.

members.name: Stone pad under the post
members.note: 6 in. The same argument as the wall's base course and the same failure if it is left out: a squared timber post set on earth rots at the ground line within a generation.

members.name: Squared and chamfered post
members.note: 7 ft. Squared from a single stick, chamfered on the arrises, and left as timber -- the portal is the one part of the building that is not earth, and it is not plastered to pretend otherwise.

members.name: Zapata -- the carved corbel bracket between post and beam
members.enrichment: scrolled, stepped or lightly gouged on the ends; the carving is the only ornament on most of these buildings
members.note: THE DIAGNOSTIC MEMBER OF THE PORTAL, and the one an imitation drops. It is a bracket that shortens the beam's clear span and spreads the bearing, so it is doing structural work and its length is set by that work rather than by taste -- which is why the carving is confined to the ends and never runs the middle. A portal whose beam sits straight on the post is not this system, whatever the post looks like. It is also the member that survives into revival work as pure decoration, applied under a beam it is not carrying, which is a different building.

members.name: Portal beam carrying the outer ends of the porch vigas
members.note: 12 in. The portal roof is a lean-to of shorter vigas from the wall head down to this beam, and its fall is the reason a portal never has a parapet on its outer edge.

invariants.note: The same move log-module makes with the foot, and for the same kind of reason: adobes were struck in moulds measured in whole inches, so the inch is the unit the system was actually built in and any other part would be a unit nobody used.

invariants.statement: The module sits inside the 10-18 in band the attested mould sizes give.
invariants.note: 10 x 14 x 4, 8 x 16 x 4 and 12 x 18 x 4 are the sizes that recur; the module is the long dimension because that is the one that crosses the wall.

invariants.statement: The wall section from floor to the top of the parapet is 9.5 modules, inside the ten-to-one slenderness limit for a wall one adobe thick.
invariants.note: This is the pack's central assertion and it is stated as an invariant rather than as a rule because it is the thing that cannot be traded away. The height-to-thickness limit is 10 in 14.7.4 NMAC and 8 in california-mission-colonial's own record, and this assembly is drawn so that it clears the tighter of the two once the wall is the two adobes a house actually has: 133 in over a 29 in wall is 4.6 to one. It clears the looser of the two even for the thinnest wall the system builds. See the height_proportion rule for why the band is left as a band.

invariants.statement: The base course is a real member and not a plinth mould: at least eight inches of stone above grade.
invariants.note: The invariant exists because this is the member most often lost when the system is imitated, and losing it is not a stylistic error -- it is the difference between a wall that stands and one that does not.

invariants.statement: The zapata is a structural member, not an applied bracket: at least a twelfth of the portal's height.
invariants.note: 112 parts of portal, so the floor is 9.33 and the encoded zapata is 10. A zapata below that depth cannot shorten the beam's span enough to be doing anything, and a bracket that is not doing anything is ornament pretending to be structure -- which is exactly what happens to the zapata in revival work.

derived_rules.authority_note: Bunting's New Mexico survey and the HABS drawings give 24-36 in for houses; spanish-colonial-american's own record gives 18 in to 5 ft across the whole tradition; mexican-colonial gives 600-1000 mm and mexican-hacienda 700-1000 mm at the base; andalusian-courtyard-vernacular gives 500-700 mm of brick, rubble or tapia.
derived_rules.note: TWO ADOBES, 28 in before the joint and about 29 with it. The number is not continuous and should never be drawn as though it were: the wall comes in whole bricks, so the real choices are about 14, about 29 and about 44 in, and a 22 in adobe wall is not a thing. The band above is wide because it has to hold the church and the placita wall as well as the house, not because the house wall is uncertain. Rammed earth is the exception and is set by the shutters, so it genuinely is continuous -- and in a tapia tradition a 20 in wall is perfectly real.

BATTER: the thickness at the wall head as a fraction of the thickness at the base. About two inches lost over a storey. Every measured section shows some of it and no source states it as a rule, because it is not one -- it is partly deliberate (a battered wall sheds water and is more stable) and partly the accumulated consequence of laying mud on mud and plastering the result by hand. It is recorded here because its ABSENCE is diagnostic: a dead-plumb wall with sharp arrises reads as insulated render on frame from fifty feet away, and no amount of colour correction recovers it. The point figure is a default inside the band and is mine, not a measurement.

derived_rules.authority_note: The reveal is the wall. Any measured section of an adobe house states this rule without meaning to.
derived_rules.note: THE ONE NUMBER THAT CANNOT BE FAKED, and the reason this pack matters more than its figures suggest. The depth of the reveal equals the thickness of the wall, because the window is a hole in a solid and there is nothing else for the reveal to be. A stucco-on-frame revival building gives 5 1/2 in and every other move on the elevation can be got right and it will still not read: the shadow at every opening is a fifth of the depth it should be, the sun never leaves a reveal in shade all day, and the eye reads the wall as a surface rather than as a mass. If one figure from this pack is carried into a drawing, carry this one.

derived_rules.authority_note: Ten times the thickness of a two-adobe wall, which is 24 ft 2 in; 14.7.4 NMAC caps unbraced wall length by the same kind of ratio and lands at very nearly the same figure.
derived_rules.note: THE CENTRAL CONSEQUENCE OF THE WHOLE SYSTEM, and the exact analogue of the log pen's sixteen feet. An earth wall standing free for more than about ten times its own thickness will fail out of plane, so it must be braced -- by a cross wall, by a buttress, or by turning a corner. That is why an adobe building is a CHAIN: a range of rooms about 24 ft long apiece whose party walls are not partitions but structure, added end to end and turned at the corner to make the placita. It is why there is no large room, why the plan grows by accretion rather than by design, and why a great room in an adobe house is a contradiction that has to be answered with steel and then explained. The 20 in the expression is 10 x 2 modules and moves with wall thickness: a church wall of three adobes may run 36 ft, and california-mission-colonial's own record answers the same arithmetic with buttresses where it cannot.

derived_rules.authority_note: 14.7.4 NMAC states 10 for unstabilised adobe. california-mission-colonial's own defining_characteristics states 8 -- 'buttresses or thickened piers wherever wall height exceeds roughly eight times wall thickness'.
derived_rules.note: MAXIMUM WALL HEIGHT AS A MULTIPLE OF WALL THICKNESS, and the band is a real disagreement rather than an averaging. The code says ten and the mission fabric says eight, and both are honest: the code is written for a wall with a modern bond beam tying its head, and the mission builders had no bond beam and answered the difference with buttresses. Where a design has a continuous reinforced bond beam, ten. Where it does not, eight, and buttress. This is a CEILING and not a generator, and the distinction is worth stating because it is the commonest way this rule is misread: for a house-scale wall of two adobes it is nowhere near binding -- a 29 in wall could stand 20 ft and the house is 11 -- so nothing about a house's height is derived from it. It binds for the single-adobe outbuilding, the placita wall, and the church. What actually sets a house's wall height is the viga and the ceiling, which is the ceiling_height_rule below.

derived_rules.authority_note: new-mexico-adobe's own record: 'Ceiling 7 ft 6 in - 9 ft 0 in to the underside of the vigas'.
derived_rules.note: Eight feet, measured TO THE UNDERSIDE OF THE VIGAS, and the qualification is the whole point: there is no ceiling plane above them. The vigas, the latillas between them and the earth on top are the ceiling, the floor above and the roof, all one construction, and the room's clear height is to the lowest of them. Anyone who draws a flat ceiling at 8 ft and vigas below it has drawn a house 9 ft 6 in tall with a decorative log stuck to the underside, and the elevation will not close.

derived_rules.authority_note: new-mexico-adobe: 'Room clear width 12-16 ft (viga span), length 1.5-2.5 times the width'. room-vernacular's reconstructed band for beam-limited vernacular traditions is 14-18 ft, and the two agree to within the difference between a peeled log and a sawn joist.
derived_rules.note: THE VIGA SPAN, and it governs the plan the way the log length governs a pen. Fourteen feet clear on the default. The consequence is that the house is SINGLE-PILE and stays single-pile: a second run of rooms behind the first needs a second bearing wall to carry a second run of vigas, which is why an adobe house grows in length and around a court rather than in depth, and why a double-pile adobe plan should be read as two ranges rather than as one deep block. The room's length then runs 1.5 to 2.5 times its width because that is what you get when the width is fixed and the only way to make a room bigger is to make it longer.

derived_rules.authority_note: new-mexico-adobe: 'roof fall 1/4 in per ft to canales'.
derived_rules.note: A quarter inch to the foot, which is 1 in 48. The roof is not flat and was never flat; it is a shallow basin falling to chosen points. The band runs from an eighth to a half inch per foot -- below an eighth the earth roof ponds and a ponded earth roof is a dissolving one, and above a half the fall shows on the parapet line from the ground. Note that this is a fall and not a pitch in the sense the slot's other users mean: a plan that reads this figure as a roof slope and draws a 1-in-48 gable has made a nonsense, and the roof_form slot must say flat-with-parapet for this rule to mean anything.

Twenty-one inches above the finished roof surface. The parapet is a drainage member before it is a compositional one -- see the wall_section assembly note. Compositionally it is also what gives these buildings their one hard horizontal line, and it is the line the eye uses to read the additive plan, because each added range brings its own parapet at its own height and the steps between them are the record of how the house grew.

derived_rules.authority_note: Half the thickness of a two-adobe wall, from the surviving canales; the requirement it answers is McHenry's.
derived_rules.note: HOW FAR THE CANALE STICKS OUT, and it is the figure that decides whether the wall below it survives. A canale is a trough cut through the parapet, timber or sheet-lined, and its whole job is to throw the water clear of the plaster. A short one does not throw clear, the water runs back down the face, and the wall dissolves in a vertical stripe under every canale -- which is what you are looking at in most photographs of a decayed adobe. Fourteen inches on the default. Longer is better and looks worse, and that trade is real and should be made deliberately rather than by default.

derived_rules.authority_note: new-mexico-adobe: adobe 'laid in moulded sun-dried brick on a stone footing'; mexican-hacienda: walls 'on a raised stone or brick socle'.
derived_rules.note: The stone or fired-brick base course, carried a foot above grade. See the base_course member for why it is not optional. Note that this is the one place where the mass-wall traditions differ visibly among themselves: New Mexico buries the footing and mud-plasters over it so the wall appears to grow out of the ground, while the Mexican hacienda and the Andalusian house express the socle as a stated, often contrasting band. Both are correct for their own node and the pack does not choose between them -- the expression slot is where a kit says which.

derived_rules.authority_note: new-mexico-adobe: 'Window opening 2 ft - 3 ft wide'. The pier rule is McHenry's and is the structural reading of the same fact.
derived_rules.note: MAXIMUM OPENING WIDTH, 35 in on the default, and less is better. Two rules travel with it and neither has a slot of its own. First, the pier of wall between two openings must be at least the wall's own thickness, so a two-adobe wall cannot carry openings closer than about 29 in apart -- which is why a run of windows, a corner window and a window turning a corner are all impossible here, and why the openings on an adobe elevation are isolated events rather than a rhythm. Second, an opening's lintel needs a bearing of at least the wall thickness at each end, so a 35 in opening consumes about 93 in of wall before anything else can happen in it.

derived_rules.authority_note: new-mexico-adobe: 'Window opening 2 ft - 3 ft wide x 3 ft - 4 ft high'.
derived_rules.note: Height over width, and squarer than any Anglo-American norm -- 1.4 against the 1.6-1.8 a double-hung sash wants. The reason is the wall: width is capped by the pier rule and height by the sill, which sits high because the wall below it is working. The consequence for a revival design is that dropping a stock double-hung unit into an adobe opening produces either a window that is too tall for its wall or a wall that has been thinned to take it, and the second is usually what happened.

derived_rules.authority_note: Hewn timber lintels in surviving New Mexico and Californian work run 6-10 in deep over domestic openings; the depth follows the span.
derived_rules.note: THE LINTEL, and it is timber in a masonry wall, which is why this rule is on window_head_masonry and reads slightly wrong there. The slot is the corpus's home for what closes the head of an opening in a mass wall, and in this tradition that is always a squared or hewn stick -- there is no arch, no relieving arch and no flat-arch gauged work anywhere in the domestic fabric, and drawing one is the single fastest way to turn an adobe house into a Mediterranean Revival one. Depth follows span at roughly one to three and a half, so 8 in over a 28 in opening. What the rule cannot say, and what matters as much, is the BEARING: at least the wall's thickness at each end, because a short-bearing lintel crushes the adobe beneath it, and crushed bearings under lintels are the commonest structural failure in a surviving adobe house.

A JUDGMENT SLOT, and the one where this system and a contemporary brief collide hardest. Nine per cent of the wall as glass, against the 15-25 per cent a modern house takes for granted and the 8 per cent minimum that most residential codes require of a habitable room's floor area -- which is a different denominator and is worth checking separately, because a deep room behind a 6 per cent wall can fail it. Everything about the tradition pushes the number down: every opening weakens a bearing wall, glass was carried by wagon and was the most expensive thing in the building, and the whole thermal strategy is a heavy skin with small holes. Everything about a client pushes it up. The pack supplies 9 per cent and defers, because there is no defensible way to say from here which of those two arguments should win in a given house -- but a design that lands above 12 per cent should stop calling the result an adobe proportion and say what it is instead.

THE PORTAL, ten feet deep on the default. It is deep for a reason that is climatic rather than social: at these latitudes a ten-foot portal on the south shades the wall and the openings behind it completely through the summer and lets the winter sun onto them, and the wall it shades is the one storing the day's heat. A four-foot porch is decoration; a ten-foot portal is part of the environmental system, and shortening it is a thermal decision disguised as a compositional one. It is also the outdoor room the plan actually uses, which is why the placita is ringed by portales rather than open to the rooms.

derived_rules.authority_note: new-mexico-adobe: 'Portal depth 8-12 ft, posts at 6-9 ft on centre'. Post sections in surviving portales run 6-9 in square.
derived_rules.note: A seven-inch squared post, chamfered, on a stone pad, carrying a zapata. Posts are set 6-9 ft on centre and -- this is the part that a composition-minded designer will fight -- their spacing is NOT aligned with the openings in the wall behind them. new-mexico-adobe states it outright: 'the two systems are independent and the tradition never reconciles them.' The portal is a timber frame set to its own beam spans and the wall is a mass structure set to its own pier rule, and they were built by different logics at different times. Regularising them produces something that looks like this tradition and reads like a stage set, because the accidental relation between post and opening is one of the things the eye is actually using.

derived_rules.authority_note: new-mexico-adobe records 'the corner fogon' as a defining element; the width band is read off surviving examples and no source states it as a rule.
derived_rules.note: THE CORNER FOGON, measured across the chord it cuts off the corner. Forty-two inches on the default. It is built of adobe with a shallow beehive hood and a small round or arched opening, it stands ACROSS the corner rather than against a wall, and it never has a chimney breast projecting into the room -- because a bearing earth wall cannot carry a flue through it and cannot carry a projecting mass hung off it either. That is the whole explanation of a detail that usually gets explained as a stylistic preference. It also means the fireplace does not organise the room the way an Anglo-American hearth wall does: it takes a corner, it heats by radiation from its own mass, and the room's furniture is arranged to the portal door and the window rather than to it. The figure is a default inside a band read off examples, and the pack defers on it.

conflicts.statement: An earth wall is a thermal mass and a very poor insulator, and the two are constantly confused. Adobe runs about R-0.25 per inch, so a 29 in wall is about R-7 as an assembly, against prescriptive requirements of R-13 to R-20 in the climate zones these buildings occupy. The mass genuinely works -- in a high desert with a 30-degree diurnal swing a heavy wall with small openings is a better building than a light insulated one, and the surviving houses are comfortable -- but it works by storing and delaying heat, not by resisting its passage, and it stops working the moment the swing narrows or the season turns. No prescriptive path will pass this wall, and the mass credits in the code do not close a thirteen-point gap.
conflicts.resolution: A performance path, and an honest one. The mass wall's real advantage is measurable in an hourly simulation and invisible in a steady-state R-value calculation, so model it rather than argue it; in a genuine high-desert climate the simulation usually wins. Where it does not, the choices are exterior insulation, which destroys the reveal and the batter and therefore the building, or interior insulation, which keeps the exterior right and throws away the mass that was the point -- and if you are throwing away the mass you should be asking why the wall is earth. The defensible middle is to insulate the roof and floor hard, keep the wall as it is, accept the wall as a stated exception in the energy model, and buy the rest back on glazing area rather than on the wall. That last move is why the daylight_strategy rule is a judgment slot.

conflicts.statement: Unreinforced earth masonry is brittle, heavy and weak in tension, which is the worst combination there is in an earthquake, and every region this pack covers is seismic. New Mexico is moderate; coastal and southern California, where the mission and Monterey fabric is, is not. Unreinforced adobe has killed people in every major Californian earthquake and the surviving colonial buildings there are almost all retrofitted. A modern building official will not permit an unreinforced bearing adobe wall in a high-seismic zone, and should not.
conflicts.resolution: A continuous reinforced bond beam at the wall head, tying every wall to every other and giving the roof diaphragm something to be fixed to, plus vertical reinforcement at corners and openings. This is standard, it is what 14.7.4 NMAC assumes when it allows ten to one, and it is invisible if the parapet is carried above it -- which is one of several reasons the parapet is a real member and not a screen. What is NOT acceptable is drawing the bond beam as an exposed concrete band, which turns the wall head into a stated line the tradition does not have; hide it, or build the parapet in adobe in front of it. On an existing building, retrofit is a conservation problem with its own literature and the answer is never to add stiffness without adding tie.

conflicts.statement: The trade is nearly gone. Unstabilised adobe is made at volume in a handful of yards in New Mexico and almost nowhere else; a mason who can lay a wall, turn a corner and run mud plaster is rare and expensive; rammed earth needs shuttering and a crew who have done it before. What the market offers instead is cement stucco on a frame wall, and it is offered specifically as this style. Every diagnostic in this pack is deleted by that substitution at once: the reveal goes from 29 in to 5 1/2, the batter goes to dead plumb, the base course has nothing to protect and disappears, the canale becomes a scupper or a decoy with a downspout behind it, the parapet becomes a screen, the wall no longer has the mass that explained the small openings so the openings grow, and the zapata becomes a bracket carrying nothing.
conflicts.resolution: Two honest paths and no third, exactly as with log. Either build the wall in earth -- and if the budget only reaches part of the building, build the street and courtyard walls in earth and frame the back, which is what a poorer owner would have done anyway -- or build in frame and keep the PROPORTIONS while declining the ones that are lies. A frame building with 24 ft structural bays, single-pile ranges around a court, a ten-foot portal on real posts with real zapatas, small high windows at nine per cent, a flat roof with real canales, and jambs furred out to give a genuinely deep reveal is a good building and an honest one. A frame building with a plumb wall, a five-inch reveal and a plastic canale is neither, and the tell is that it is TOO GOOD: too plumb, too straight, too even in colour. These walls were laid by eye and finished by hand and they are not straight, and the imitation is caught precisely by its perfection.

conflicts.statement: The roof is a rainfall-specific device and it does not travel. A flat earth roof drained by canales is a sound answer at 8-14 in of annual rainfall, mostly in short summer storms, on a site with a long dry season to recover in. Above about 20 in it is a maintenance liability, and in a climate with driving rain, freeze-thaw at the parapet, or snow that lies, it is not defensible at all. The wall has the same problem in a different form: an unstabilised earth wall in a wet climate needs a much larger roof overhang than the parapet permits, and the parapet is the one thing the composition cannot give up.
conflicts.resolution: Outside the dry belt, keep the wall and change the roof, and say so. The Iberian and Mexican traditions this pack also covers already did it -- andalusian-courtyard-vernacular and much of mexican-colonial carry a tiled pitched roof on the same mass wall, with an eave that oversails and protects it, and that is a fully authentic combination rather than a compromise. What is not defensible is carrying the New Mexico flat roof and parapet into a wet climate because it is the image people have of adobe, and then detailing around it with membrane and internal drains. If the roof must be flat, the honest modern answer is a membrane with the parapet and canales kept as the visible, functioning overflow, and the canale must still throw clear.

conflicts.statement: The wall eats the floor plan, and the arithmetic is worse than it looks because it compounds with the 24 ft bracing rule. A 40 x 30 ft footprint with a 29 in wall gives about 1,190 sf gross and about 900 sf of net interior -- roughly a quarter of the footprint is wall. At the three-adobe thickness of a church or a two-storey base it is a third. Cross walls at 24 ft centres add more, and unlike a partition they cannot be moved later, so the plan is fixed on the day the foundations are poured. Against that, the wall is also the finish inside and out, the thermal store, and the acoustic separation, and it needs no cavity, no insulation, no rainscreen and no drywall.
conflicts.resolution: Price it as net area, not gross, and tell the client that number before anything is drawn -- the shock is not the cost per square foot, it is discovering late that the house is a fifth smaller inside than the footprint said. Then use the wall for everything it can do: build the seating, the shelving, the fireplace and the deep window seats INTO its thickness, which is what these buildings do, and which recovers real usable volume from what looked like pure loss. A 29 in wall gives a 24 in seat under every window for nothing.

sources: Bainbridge Bunting, Early Architecture in New Mexico, University of New Mexico Press, Albuquerque, 1976
Paul Graham McHenry, Jr., Adobe and Rammed Earth Buildings: Design and Construction, John Wiley & Sons, New York, 1984
New Mexico Earthen Building Materials Code, 14.7.4 NMAC, Construction Industries Division, State of New Mexico
Rexford Newcomb, Spanish-Colonial Architecture in the United States, J. J. Augustin, New York, 1937
Historic American Buildings Survey, measured drawings of New Mexico and California adobe houses (HABS NM, HABS CA)
notes:
The gap this pack fills was named by four style nodes in their own binding notes -- spanish-colonial-american, new-mexico-adobe, california-mission-colonial and monterey-colonial each say in so many words that a dedicated mass-wall or adobe module is missing from the corpus and that their real, numbered constraints have no pack behind them. WP-4.1 confirmed it independently from three batches. Until now those nodes were bound to room-vernacular, which is a beam-limited vernacular ROOM system and is genuinely close on the one dimension it shares -- span-limited room width -- and says nothing whatever about a wall.

What is deliberately NOT in this pack, and why. There is no ornament system: the portada, the retablo panel and the carved doorway of the Mexican and Iberian traditions are a bounded-panel ornament logic that WP-4.1 listed separately as its own missing pack, and folding a few figures for it in here would have made this pack the place where two unrelated systems are half-stated. There is no courtyard or placita geometry beyond the bracing rule that generates it, because the placita is a plan diagram and belongs to the parti layer, where WP-4.5 has now put it. There is no figure for the mud plaster's coat thickness or its renewal cycle, because the surviving practice varies from an annual enjarre by hand to a modern stabilised render and no single number is defensible across that range.

Confidence is medium and not high, and the reason is worth stating rather than leaving in the field. The wall PHYSICS is well attested and I would defend it anywhere: the slenderness limit, the bracing length, the base course, the reveal, the lintel bearing and the canale projection are all recoverable from the fabric and from McHenry, and several of them are stated independently by the corpus's own style records. The specific point figures inside the bands -- the batter at 0.93, the fogon at 42 in, the glazed fraction at 9 per cent -- are defaults, and the three that are most mine are marked judgment: true rather than left to look like measurements.
